arc_intro:
FQ-218 — Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

WAF review put IaC at the top of the priority list for one reason: without it, the architecture exists only in manual console actions and human memory. Let's fix that.

Quick thing before we start — Deepak mentioned he made a direct console change to a security group last week for debugging. karthik-dev said 'that's fine, it's defined in our CloudFormation template so it's tracked.' I want you to check whether that statement is actually true.

— Ravi

Build the network layer for real: subnets, IGW, NAT, and non-overlapping CIDR.
arc_outro:
Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

The SG drift finding was a good reminder of why this matters — 'defined in the template' and 'deployed state matches the template' are two different things, and assuming they're the same is exactly how drift compounds quietly over time. Good catch, good fix, proper process going forward.

The CloudFormation coverage isn't complete yet — we've captured the core compute and security layer, but storage and monitoring still need their own stacks. That's fine for now, this gives us a solid starting point and a discipline for future changes.

Next: cost attribution. The tagging gap has been on the list since the WAF review — I want to be able to answer 'which team owns this cost' before the next board meeting.

— Ravi

tasks.scenario: karthik-dev says: 'Deepak's manual SG change is fine — the security group is defined in our CloudFormation template, so AWS tracks it.' You decide to check the actual deployed security group against the template before the discussion with Ravi.
tasks.question: What's wrong with karthik-dev's reasoning that 'defined in a template means AWS tracks changes to it'?
options: A) Nothing — CloudFormation automatically keeps deployed resources in sync with their template definition at all times

B) CloudFormation defines what the resource SHOULD look like when a stack is created or updated, but it does NOT automatically revert manual console changes. If someone changes a resource directly in the console, CloudFormation has no automatic mechanism to detect or undo that — the deployed state can silently diverge from the template definition until someone explicitly runs a drift detection or stack update
C) karthik-dev is correct that templates track changes, but only for security groups, not other resource types
D) CloudFormation templates are just documentation — they have no connection to actual deployed resources at all
tasks.explanation: CloudFormation's template 'what should be deployed' define does — but deployed state-a automatically sync to do manual change revert what was done. in Console manual change did, template unaware-a will be, drift silently accumulate will happen until explicitly detect they will do.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — template definition and deployed state are separate things; manual changes create silent drift.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — CloudFormation automatic sync what was done. Manual changes create drift that template doesn't know about.

tasks.question: What is 'infrastructure drift' in the context of IaC, and why is it specifically dangerous?
options: A) Drift refers to the slow performance degradation of cloud resources over time, unrelated to configuration

B) Drift is when the actual deployed state of infrastructure diverges from what the IaC template/code defines as the intended state — dangerous because it means the template is no longer a reliable picture of what's actually running, security changes may have been quietly reversed, and any future stack update might accidentally overwrite manual changes or fail unexpectedly
C) Drift only occurs when an IaC tool is outdated and needs to be upgraded
D) Drift is a normal and expected part of running infrastructure with IaC — it's considered acceptable as long as it's less than 10% of resources
tasks.explanation: Drift — deployed state vs template definition's gap — dangerous because template 'reliable picture' without aagudhu, security changes quietly reversed can be, future stack update unexpected-a fail can happen or manual changes overwrite can happen. Silent-a accumulate aagardhu real risk.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — drift is the silent gap between template and reality, dangerous because it makes the template untrustworthy.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — drift performance degradation not. Template vs deployed state's silent gap, security implications's.

tasks.question: At a high level, what's the main practical difference between CloudFormation and Terraform as IaC tools?
options: A) CloudFormation supports multiple cloud providers; Terraform only works with AWS

B) CloudFormation is AWS-native (no separate tool to install, tight AWS service integration, AWS manages the state), while Terraform is cloud-agnostic (works with AWS, GCP, Azure, and more) with its own state management that the team must maintain. Both can manage AWS infrastructure — the choice often comes down to multi-cloud needs and team familiarity
C) Terraform is owned and operated by AWS; CloudFormation is a third-party tool
D) They're functionally identical in every way — the only difference is the file format used for templates
tasks.explanation: CloudFormation AWS-native — install needed not, AWS state manage does, tight AWS integration. Terraform cloud-agnostic — AWS, GCP, Azure support does, team themselves state manage must do. Both in AWS velai does, choice multi-cloud need and team familiarity-a base after doing.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — CloudFormation AWS-native, Terraform cloud-agnostic with self-managed state. Both valid for AWS.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — providers reverse-ah. CloudFormation AWS-only, Terraform multi-cloud. AWS state management important practical difference.

tasks.scenario: karthik-dev asks: 'Should we use CloudFormation or Terraform for FoodQuick's IaC? I've seen both at previous companies.'
tasks.question: How should this decision be reasoned through for FoodQuick's specific situation?
options: A) Terraform is always better than CloudFormation for any company, regardless of context

B) For FoodQuick's current situation (AWS-only infrastructure, small team, no existing IaC at all), CloudFormation is a practical starting point — no additional tool to install or learn, no state management overhead for the team, and deep AWS service integration. Terraform becomes more relevant if FoodQuick expands to multiple cloud providers or the team has strong prior Terraform expertise. The most important thing is starting with either — the cost of no IaC (as the WAF review showed) is higher than the cost of either tool choice
C) CloudFormation is always better because it's the official AWS tool
D) The choice must be made only after consulting AWS Support, since they assign specific IaC tools to accounts
tasks.explanation: This context-based decision — FoodQuick AWS-only, small team, no existing IaC. CloudFormation practical starting point (no extra tool, AWS state management, tight integration). Terraform multi-cloud if it was or team strong familiarity-a if it was better. Most important: START with either — tool in debate time waste to do must not.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — context-based reasoning, not a universal answer. Starting matters more than which tool.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — 'always better' universal answer not. Context (AWS-only, team size, familiarity) drive must do this decision.

tasks.scenario: ananya-analyst asks: 'I've heard IaC described as idempotent. What does that actually mean in practice?'
tasks.question: What does idempotency mean for IaC, and why does it matter?
options: A) Idempotency means the template file can never be modified after it's first created

B) Idempotency means running the same IaC template multiple times produces the same result — if the infrastructure already matches the template, running it again makes no changes; if it drifted, it brings it back to the defined state. This means you can safely re-apply a template without fear of creating duplicates or causing unintended changes, making deployments predictable and repeatable
C) Idempotency is a Terraform-specific concept that doesn't apply to CloudFormation
D) Idempotency means the template automatically backs up the previous infrastructure state before making changes
tasks.explanation: Idempotency — same template multiple times run even if done same result — already matching if it was no changes, drifted-a if it was back to defined state. This deployments predictable-a, repeatable-a does — double-run panrfor that fearless-a can be.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — idempotent means same result every time, safe to re-apply without fear of duplicates.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — idempotency template-lock not. Same template multiple times same result kudukkudhu meaning.

tasks.scenario: You've removed the drifted port 22 rule manually. Now you run a CloudFormation stack update to add a small legitimate change (a tag update on all resources). The update fails.
tasks.error_shown:
CloudFormation Stack Update: FAILED
Rollback initiated

Resource: sg-order-svc-0072
Error: Unable to update security group: the requested inbound rule already exists — Port 80+443, Source: sg-alb-foodquick-order. Cannot create duplicate rule.
tasks.diagnosis: The port 22 rule was removed manually (correctly), but BEFORE running the stack update, there was still another instance of drift — something else in the SG had been modified and wasn't fully reconciled with the template. The stack update tried to apply the template's full defined state, found a rule it thought it needed to create already existed (or vice versa), and failed with a duplicate-rule conflict. This is a classic 'partial drift remediation followed by a stack update' failure mode — if any drift remains when a stack update runs, the update can conflict with the existing state in unexpected ways.
tasks.fix: Run drift detection AGAIN before running any stack update, to confirm the deployed state completely matches the template before trying to update. Never assume 'I fixed the drift I knew about' means 'all drift is gone' — drift detection is the authoritative check, not human memory of what was changed.
tasks.explanation: This real sequence-a padam panrfor that is important — drift partially fix after doing, stack update run did, remaining drift conflict create aagidhu. Drift detection authoritative check — 'I think I fixed it' insufficient. Always verify before update.

cases.case_1: FoodQuick's production VPC, subnets, route tables, and security groups
cases.case_2: The content of FoodQuick's S3 buckets (the actual image files, log files, order exports)
cases.case_3: Deepak's personal SSH key pair in the EC2 console
cases.case_4: The CloudWatch alarms for order-service (HighErrorRate, HighCPU)

correct_answers.case_1: Manage with IaC — networking resources are the most critical to have reproducibly defined; losing this to human memory in a DR scenario is the highest-risk gap in the entire stack
correct_answers.case_2: NOT managed by IaC — IaC manages the infrastructure (the bucket itself, its configuration, its lifecycle policies), not the data objects inside it. S3 object content is data, not infrastructure
correct_answers.case_3: NOT managed by IaC — personal credentials and developer access artifacts are identity/access management concerns, typically managed through IAM policies and individual access methods, not encoded into infrastructure templates
correct_answers.case_4: Manage with IaC — CloudWatch alarms are infrastructure configuration, not data. Defining them in code means alarm configuration changes are reviewed, tracked, and reproducible — not manual console clicks that can quietly drift

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks for a clear framework on what should and should not be managed through IaC templates.
tasks.explanation: Naanku different different resource type — VPC/networking (manage with IaC, highest DR risk), S3 object content (not IaC, data not infrastructure), personal credentials (not IaC, identity management), CloudWatch alarms (manage with IaC, configuration not data). This real judgment: IaC — infrastructure for configuration, for data or personal for credentials not.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — infrastructure configuration belongs in IaC; data content and personal credentials don't.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — IaC manages infrastructure configuration, not the data inside resources or personal access credentials. Distinction matters.

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks for the real cost of the drift incident — not in AWS charges (there were none), but in engineering time and security risk. The drift lasted one week. Deepak's home IP had open SSH access to the production order-service instances for that entire period.
tasks.question: How should the cost of this drift incident be framed honestly, given that nothing bad actually happened?
tasks.solution: Direct AWS cost: ₹0 — no infrastructure was harmed, no charges changed. Real cost has two components: (1) Engineering time: approximately 3-4 hours total (discovering drift, deciding what to do, removing the rule, resolving the stack update conflict, documenting the process) at ₹2,500/hour ≈ ₹7,500-10,000. (2) Risk cost: one week of open SSH access from an external IP to production order-service instances — this could have been discovered and exploited by a scanner or attacker during that window. The ₹42L comparable security incident from FQ-189 (driver-documents) illustrates what 'window of external access to production systems' can cost when noticed by the wrong party. Framed honestly: this drift cost almost nothing this time, but the same pattern (manual change creating a silent security gap) is the same root cause as FQ-189's six-week driver-documents exposure. The process fix has real value.
tasks.explanation: Drift incidents often cost nothing until they cost everything — honest framing is 'near-miss with a real risk window,' not 'nothing happened so no real cost.' Process fix value is prevention of the next incident, not remediation of this one.
